claims.text: The magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys is primarily governed by local microstructural strain and grain-boundary density.
Local strain and grain boundaries pin magnetic domains during the first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The stated as-deposited initial state is produced by arc melting or melt spinning.
The initial microstructure has fine grains and significant residual internal strain.
Moderate-temperature annealing can promote grain growth and relax internal strain without causing phase separation or oxidation.
Annealing at approximately 550°C for 1–5 hours in an inert atmosphere will reduce grain-boundary density.
Annealing at approximately 550°C for 1–5 hours in an inert atmosphere will relieve local lattice strain.
Annealing-induced grain growth and strain relaxation decrease the density of magnetic-domain-wall pinning sites.
Reducing local lattice distortions smooths the abrupt first-order magnetostructural transition.
Smoothing the magnetostructural transition reduces magnetocaloric hysteresis.
Smoothing the magnetostructural transition broadens its temperature range.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will have lower hysteresis in magnetization cycles.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will exhibit a broader transition and a modestly lower peak entropy change.
The annealed samples will show improved reversibility during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited fine-grained, highly strained baseline produces a large, sharp, and hysteretic magnetocaloric entropy change.
The predictions apply only under low-field cooling conditions and while annealing preserves the original phase.
Secondary-phase formation or oxidation at excessive annealing temperatures or durations could invalidate the predicted behavior.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly called 'as-deposited,' but its initial state is said to be produced by arc melting or melt spinning. Arc melting produces a bulk ingot rather than a deposited state, and the hypothesis does not identify an actual deposition process.
